title: A Case of Spontaneous Remission of Non‐Hodgkin's Lymphoma in the Lung
content:
ABSTRACTA 72‐year‐old male with a lung lesion was diagnosed with non‐Hodgkin's lymphoma through percutaneous needle lung biopsy. The patient's lung tumor disappeared during follow‐up 4 months later without any standard antitumor treatments. This is a rare case of spontaneous tumor remission.

Summary Spontaneous remission (SR) of cancer is a rare biological event.Infection, biopsy procedures, and tumor microenvironment may be potential mechanisms for SR.Presenting a rare case of spontaneous remission of primary pulmonary non‐Hodgkin's lymphoma. 1Case PresentationA 72‐year‐old male had abnormal CEA and CA19‐9 levels for 7 years, with annual gastroscopies showing no malignant lesions. Additionally, he had a 3‐year history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), managed conservatively due to mild symptoms. In 2023, his wheezing worsened from a COVID‐19 infection. On June 20, 2023, a PET‐CT scan revealed increased metabolic activity in a mixed ground glass density nodule in the right lower lobe (SUVmax ≈ 4.8; size ≈ 2.0 × 2.2 cm), indicating a malignant lung tumor. Due to surgical treatment intolerance, conservative management with traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) was chosen. Oral pirfenidone began on July 27th but was changed to nintedanib in October due to unsatisfactory symptom improvement. A CT‐guided percutaneous lung lesion biopsy was performed on November 23, revealing non‐Hodgkin's lymphoma derived from B cells. Immunohistochemical results showed CK (AE1/AE3) (−), CK5/6 (−), TTF‐1 (+), CD3 (reactive T cells+), CD5 (reactive T cells+), CD20 (L26) (diffuse+), CD79a (diffuse+), CD21 (FDC+), CD23 (FDC+), Ki67 (MIB‐1) (40%+), CD138 (+), CD38 (+), lgG (+), and lgG4 (−) (see Figure 1). In situ hybridization revealed EBER (−). Genetic testing detected clonal gene rearrangements of IGH and IGK, but not TCRG, TCRD, or TCRB. On March 21, 2024, he returned to our department for a chest CT due to worsening dyspnea. Surprisingly, the CT showed the tumor had disappeared (see Figure 2). Two months later, the patient accidentally fell and fractured the rib cage. Chest CT was rechecked, and no tumor recurrence was found.FIGURE 1Pathology images from the CT‐guided biopsy. (a) HE staining, magnified 400×. (b) CD20 result, magnified 100×. (c) Ki67 result, magnified 100×.FIGURE 2Changes in lesions on chest CT before and after biopsy. (a) Before biopsy. Nodular lesion in the lower right lung (se303 im251), with a length of approximately 25 × 26 mm, on October 7, 2023 (256 row CT). (b) Four months after biopsy. No visible nodule in the lower right lung, on March 21, 2024 (16 row CT). (c) Follow‐up for another 2 months. No recurrence was observed, on June 12, 2024 (256 row CT).2What Caused the SR of the Tumor in This Case?The biopsy is considered the possible cause.3DiscussionSpontaneous remission (SR) of cancer is a rare biological event proposed in 1956. Lymphoma is a common SR cancer type. Given SR's low incidence, we encountered a more rare case: Primary pulmonary non‐Hodgkin's lymphoma comprises only 0.4% of all lymphomas [1]. Fever and infection, which stimulate an immune response, may promote SR [2]. Biopsy and ablation procedures, which disrupt the tumor microenvironment, may also induce SR [2]. As in our case, biopsy is easily assumed the main cause of regression. There are also some case reports of cancer SR after TCM treatment [3]. Although the patients in our case also used Chinese Herbs as an alternative treatment, due to limited data, its exact effect cannot be evaluated yet.The case had a long history of high CEA that significantly declined before biopsy (see Figure 3). If we follow monism, it is difficult to define the relationships between CEA and pulmonary lymphoma, as well as CA19‐9, since they are generally believed to have a stronger correlation with digestive system tumors. However, there are no signs or evidence of other related diseases.FIGURE 3Changes in tumor markers and timing of biopsy. CEA decreased before the biopsy and tended to be stable, while Ca19‐9 rebounded.The duration of remission remains to be observed. Poor lung function (SPO2 = 92%) caused by COPD and IPF significantly impacts survival unfavorably.Author Contributions Sun Li: resources, visualization, writing – original draft, writing – review and editing. Fan Hong Yu: writing – review and editing. Shi Yanfen: resources, writing – review and editing.Ethics StatementMedical Ethics Committee of Puyang Traditional Chinese Medicine Hospital approved the research. Ethical approval No. 202312. The study has obtained informed consent from the patient.ConsentWritten informed consent was obtained from the patient to publish this report in accordance with the journal's patient consent policy.Conflicts of InterestThe authors declare no conflicts of interest.

diagnosis.diagnosis_raw: Non‐Hodgkin's lymphoma in the lung (primary pulmonary non-Hodgkin's lymphoma), derived from B cells.
diagnosis.quality_of_life_impact: Worsening dyspnea; poor lung function with SPO2 = 92% in setting of COPD and IPF.
diagnosis.disease_duration_before_healing: Approximately 4 months after biopsy the tumor disappeared (biopsy 2023-11-23 to CT 2024-03-21).
diagnosis.cancer_subtype: Primary pulmonary non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, B-cell derived

treatment.treatments_raw: No standard antitumor treatments were given; not a surgical candidate. CT-guided percutaneous biopsy performed.
treatment.treatment_stopped_reason: Not treated with standard antitumor therapy due to surgical intolerance; managed conservatively.
treatment.alternative_treatments_raw: Conservative management with traditional Chinese medicine (Chinese herbs).

remission_outcome.time_to_remission_raw: Tumor disappeared on CT about 4 months after biopsy.
remission_outcome.verification_detail: Biopsy on 2023-11-23 confirmed B-cell non-Hodgkin's lymphoma; follow-up chest CT on 2024-03-21 showed no visible nodule; repeat CT on 2024-06-12 showed no recurrence.
remission_outcome.tumor_response: Disappearance of the lung tumor on CT.
remission_outcome.tumor_size_change: Approx. 2.0 × 2.2 cm (PET-CT June 2023) / approx. 25 × 26 mm on CT 2023-10-07 to no visible nodule on CT 2024-03-21.
remission_outcome.biomarker_trajectory: CEA decreased before biopsy and tended to be stable; CA19-9 rebounded (no numeric values provided).
remission_outcome.follow_up_duration_raw: No recurrence on CT 2 months later (June 12, 2024).

agency_examples: Chose conservative management due to intolerance of surgical treatment
Used traditional Chinese medicine as an alternative approach
turner_factors.agency_details: Opted for conservative management rather than surgery; used TCM.

validation.statistical_improbability_notes: Primary pulmonary non-Hodgkin's lymphoma is rare (~0.4% of lymphomas) and lesion disappeared without standard antitumor therapy after biopsy.
validation.extraction_notes: Remission durability beyond ~2-4 months post-disappearance is not established; no numeric tumor marker values provided.

analysis.case_summary: A 72-year-old man with a right lower lobe lung lesion had B-cell non-Hodgkin's lymphoma confirmed by CT-guided biopsy (2023-11-23). Without standard antitumor therapy, follow-up CT four months later (2024-03-21) showed complete disappearance of the tumor, with no recurrence on CT two months after that (2024-06-12).
key_healing_factors: Spontaneous regression temporally following CT-guided percutaneous biopsy (authors propose biopsy-triggered regression)
Use of traditional Chinese medicine/chinese herbs (effect uncertain per authors)
unique_features: Primary pulmonary non-Hodgkin's lymphoma with complete radiographic disappearance without standard antitumor treatment
Detailed immunohistochemistry and clonal IGH/IGK rearrangement supporting diagnosis
Regression occurred after biopsy, suggesting procedure-related immune/microenvironment disruption
analysis.analysis_notes: Narrative focuses on biomedical mechanisms (biopsy, infection, tumor microenvironment) and does not report psycho-spiritual changes or anomalous experiences. Conventional anti-cancer therapies were not administered; antifibrotics (pirfenidone/nintedanib) were used for IPF and are not anti-lymphoma treatments.
